# Book II, Proposition 3

*The rectangle contained by the whole and one segment*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> If a straight line be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments and the square on the aforesaid segment.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it · Euclid's argument

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/II/03.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition II.3, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For let the straight line AB be cut at random at C;

I say that the rectangle contained by AB, BC is equal to the rectangle contained by AC, CB together with the square on BC.

For let the square CDEB be described on CB; [I. 46]

let ED be drawn through to F,

and through A let AF be drawn parallel to either CD or BE. [I. 31]

Then AE is equal to AD, CE.

Now AE is the rectangle contained by AB, BC, for it is contained by AB, BE, and BE is equal to BC;

AD is the rectangle AC, CB, for DC is equal to CB;

and DB is the square on CB.

Therefore the rectangle contained by AB, BC is equal to the rectangle contained by AC, CB together with the square on BC.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

From [`Elements/BookII/Prop03.lean`](../../Elements/BookII/Prop03.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out. The list below marks where a lemma does a step Euclid takes for granted; the `/- … -/` notes in the listing explain smaller adjustments.

**How the Lean follows the text**

- **Done by `BookI.Prop31.parallelogram`.** "and through A let AF be drawn parallel…" Euclid draws AF parallel to CD and takes its meeting with DE at F from the figure. `BookI.Prop31.parallelogram` draws the parallel by I.31, finds F by `BookI.Prop30.meet` and proves DCAF a parallelogram; `BookI.Prop30.parallel` (I.30, for which Heath gives no reference here) makes AF parallel to BE as well.
- **Done by `quadArea_add_of_parallelograms`.** "Then AE is equal to AD, CE." Euclid takes AE as AD and CE together. `Parallel.between` places D between F and E, and `quadArea_add_of_parallelograms` proves that AFDC and CDEB make up AFEB.
- **Done by `Rectangle.of_right`.** "Now AE is the rectangle contained by AB, BC…" Euclid treats AE as a rectangle, with BE equal to BC. The Lean proves BAFE a parallelogram, carries the square's right angle at B along BA, and uses `Rectangle.of_right` (I.29) and `Rectangle.eq_rect` to identify its area.
- **Done by `Rectangle.of_right`.** "AD is the rectangle AC, CB…" Euclid treats AD as a rectangle, with DC equal to CB. The Lean gets the adjacent right angle at C from `Tacit.adjacent_eq_of_right` (I.13), then uses `Rectangle.of_right` (I.29) and `Rectangle.eq_rect` to identify AD.

```lean
/-- If a straight line be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the
segments is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments and the square on the aforesaid
segment. -/
theorem Prop3 {A B C : Point} (hACB : Between A C B) :
    rect A B B C = rect A C C B + sq B C := by
  -- For let the straight line AB be cut at random at C;
  have hAB : A ≠ B := ne_of_between_ends hACB
  have hAC : A ≠ C := ne_of_between hACB
  have hCB : C ≠ B := (ne_of_between (between_symm hACB)).symm
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
  have hC_AB : OnLine C AB := on_line_of_between_ends hACB hA_AB hB_AB
  -- I say that the rectangle contained by AB, BC is equal to the rectangle contained by AC, CB
  -- together with the square on BC.
  -- For let the square CDEB be described on CB; [I. 46]
  /- I.46 describes the square on the side of a point off CB (`exists_off_line`), and
     `Square.described` says it is the square on CB. -/
  obtain ⟨P, hP, -⟩ := exists_off_line hCB []
  obtain ⟨D, E, hsq, hD, hE⟩ := BookI.Prop46 hCB hP
  obtain ⟨hp, hDB⟩ := Square.described hsq hD hE
  -- let ED be drawn through to F,
  /- DE names the whole straight line. The parallel through A will find F on it. -/
  obtain ⟨DE, hD_DE, hE_DE⟩ := Postulate1 D E hp.2.1
  have hDE_AB : Parallel DE AB := hp.2.parallel hD_DE hE_DE hB_AB hC_AB
  -- and through A let AF be drawn parallel to either CD or BE. [I. 31]
  /- I.31 draws AF parallel to CD; I.30 finds its meeting with DE and makes it
     parallel to BE as well. -/
  obtain ⟨CD, hC_CD, hD_CD⟩ := Postulate1 C D hp.1.1
  obtain ⟨BE, hB_BE, hE_BE⟩ := Postulate1 B E hp.1.2.1.symm
  have hCD_BE : Parallel CD BE := hp.1.parallel hC_CD hD_CD hE_BE hB_BE
  obtain ⟨F, hF_DE, hDCAF⟩ :=
    BookI.Prop31.parallelogram hDE_AB hD_DE hC_AB hA_AB hAC.symm
  have hAF : A ≠ F := hDCAF.1.2.1
  obtain ⟨AF, hA_AF, hF_AF⟩ := Postulate1 A F hAF
  have hAF_CD : Parallel AF CD := (hDCAF.1.parallel hD_CD hC_CD hA_AF hF_AF).symm
  have hA_BE : ¬ OnLine A BE := fun h =>
    hCD_BE.not_onLine hC_CD ((line_unique hAB hA_AB hB_AB h hB_BE) ▸ hC_AB)
  have hAF_BE : Parallel AF BE :=
    BookI.Prop30.parallel hAF_CD hCD_BE.symm fun e => hA_BE (e ▸ hA_AF)
  -- Then AE is equal to AD, CE.
  /- Parallels keep order: D lies between F and E, as C lies between A and B.
     Thus CD cuts the whole AFEB into AFDC and CDEB. -/
  have hFDE : Between F D E :=
    Parallel.between hAF_CD hCD_BE.symm hA_AF hC_CD hB_BE hACB hF_AF hD_CD hE_BE
      ⟨DE, hF_DE, hD_DE, hE_DE⟩
  have hAFDC : Parallelogram A F D C := hDCAF.rotate.rotate
  have hwhole : quadArea A F E B = quadArea A F D C + quadArea C D E B :=
    quadArea_add_of_parallelograms hAFDC hp hACB hFDE
  -- Now AE is the rectangle contained by AB, BC, for it is contained by AB, BE, and BE is
  -- equal to BC;
  /- AE is the parallelogram BAFE, and its angle at B is the square's right angle, so it
     is a rectangle (`Rectangle.of_right`), contained by AB and BE (`Rectangle.eq_rect`). -/
  have hFE : F ≠ E := ne_of_between_ends hFDE
  have hBAFE : Parallelogram B A F E :=
    ⟨AreParallel.of_parallel hAB.symm hFE hB_AB hA_AB hF_DE hE_DE hDE_AB.symm,
      AreParallel.of_parallel hAF hp.1.2.1 hA_AF hF_AF hE_BE hB_BE hAF_BE⟩
  have hAE : quadArea A F E B = rect A B B C := by
    rw [hBAFE.quadArea_rotate]
    refine (Rectangle.of_right hBAFE ?_).eq_rect (len_symm B A) ?_
    · rw [angle_onRay_right (OnRay.of_beyond (between_symm hACB)) hp.1.2.1]
      exact hsq.2.2.2.2.2.2
    · rw [len_symm B E]; exact hsq.2.2.1
  -- AD is the rectangle AC, CB, for DC is equal to CB;
  have hAD : quadArea A F D C = rect A C C B := by
    have hCAFD : Parallelogram C A F D := hDCAF.rotate
    rw [hCAFD.quadArea_rotate]
    have hD_AB : ¬ OnLine D AB := hDE_AB.not_onLine hD_DE
    /- The angle DCA adjacent to the square's right angle BCD is right
       (I.13, `adjacent_eq_of_right`). -/
    have hright : ∠ D C A = ∟ := by
      have h := hsq.2.2.2.1
      rw [adjacent_eq_of_right hB_AB hA_AB (between_symm hACB) hD_AB h] at h
      exact h
    exact (Rectangle.of_right hCAFD hright).eq_rect (len_symm C A) hsq.len_eq.symm
  -- and DB is the square on CB.
  have hDB' : quadArea C D E B = sq B C := hDB.trans (sq_symm C B)
  -- Therefore the rectangle contained by AB, BC is equal to the rectangle contained by AC, CB
  -- together with the square on BC.
  rw [← hAE, hwhole, hAD, hDB']
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L52): **Superposition.** A hypothetical placement of a triangle on a given ray and side permits a restricted derivation of metric equalities about the figure already given. The derivation introduces no further objects, cites each geometric law it uses, and exports no symbol of the placement.

(System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L35) (through [`BookI.Prop31.parallelogram`](../../Elements/BookI/HelpersParallels.lean#L83), [`OnRay.of_beyond`](../../Elements/Figure/Rays.lean#L41), [`Parallel.between`](../../Elements/Figure/Parallelograms.lean#L101) and 10 other lemmas): What is less than the less is less still. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L39) (through [`BookI.Prop31.parallelogram`](../../Elements/BookI/HelpersParallels.lean#L83), [`OnRay.of_beyond`](../../Elements/Figure/Rays.lean#L41), [`Parallel.between`](../../Elements/Figure/Parallelograms.lean#L101) and 10 other lemmas): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. ## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

Euclid describes the square CDEB on CB, and then calls it by two other names: CE, when it is added to AD to make AE, and DB, when it is the square on CB. He names a figure by two opposite corners, so AE is AFEB and AD is AFDC. "Let ED be drawn through to F" names F before saying where it lies. In our foundations a straight line is already the whole straight line, so when we name DE it is drawn through, and the parallel through A meets it at F.

Leave Book II itself aside and look to general use, Heath says, and this proposition and II.2 are "of great importance, and particularly so to the semi-algebraical method just described, which seems to have found its first exponents in Heron and Pappus" (vol. 1, p. 378). Euclid uses II.3 again in IX.15, and Pappus often quotes it by its book and number, as Heath remarks under II.2 (vol. 1, p. 377). Heath's example of the method is Dionysius Lardner's proof, by II.1 to II.3 alone, that "*the difference of the squares on two straight lines is equal to the rectangle contained by the sum and the difference of the straight lines*" (vol. 1, pp. 378–379), a theorem generally given as equivalent to II.5 and II.6. II.2 makes the square on AB the rectangles AB, BC and AB, AC; II.3 takes the square on BC out of the first; and II.1 joins the two rectangles left over into one, contained by AC, the difference, and the sum of AB and BC.

**The modern way.** Euclid's figure draws $(a + b)a = ab + a^2$, with $\mathrm{CB} = a$ and $\mathrm{AC} = b$: the rectangle AE cut along CD into the rectangle AD and the square. It is the third of the identities Heath lists for Book II. Lardner's theorem, with $p = \mathrm{AB}$ and $q = \mathrm{BC}$, is $p^2 - q^2 = (p - q)(p + q)$.

## Further reading

- Thomas L. Heath's [*A History of Greek Mathematics*, vol. 2](https://archive.org/details/cu31924008704227) (1921, free online) gives a chapter each to Heron and Pappus, whom his note here takes for the first exponents of the semi-algebraical method.
- Teachers and editors reworked Euclid's proofs for centuries, as Dionysius Lardner does in Heath's note here, and Benjamin Wardhaugh's [*Encounters with Euclid*](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691211695/encounters-with-euclid) (2021) is a history of the *Elements* told through such people, who copied, translated, taught and argued over it.
